newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin defends veto of religion bill,Church upset.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin defends veto of religion bill,Church upset.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin on Wednesday defended his decision to veto a controversial bill to curb religious freedoms inn Russia, but a top cleric expressed dismay at the move.

Yeltsin threw out the draft law "On Freedom of Conscience and Religious Association" on Tuesday. He said it contravened Russia's post-Soviet constitution guaranteeing equality for all confessions and also its international pledges on human rights.

The Kremlin press service issued a statement saying he president had sent an explanation to the chairmen of Russia's two houses of parliament -- which now both need a two-thirds majority to override the veto.
"In the letter it is noted that the draft law contradicts the basis of the Russian Federation's constitution...and generally accepted principles and norms of international law," the statement said.
But Archbishop Sergiy of the Russian Orthodox Church's Holy Synod told Itar-Tass news agency that all Orthodox believers would be disappointed.
"From our point of view the law...objectively reflected the religious situation in the country. (The veto) evokes great regret and surprise among Orthodox people," he said.

The bill, approved by a majority of parliamentarians and strongly backed by the Orthodox Church, had stirred fears among human rights groups and minority religious groups that Russia was returning to Soviet-style state control of worship.
The United States and Pope John Paul II had also expressed concern for religious freedom in Russia.

But supporters argued the bill would help curb the sects that have proliferated in Russia in recent years, exploiting people's spiritual confusion and curiosity after decades of totalitarian communist rule.
"Of course the state can and must limit the activity of pseudo-religious organisations that bring harm to the morality and health of the population," Yeltsin's statement said.
"But this does not mean that the state can trample on fundamental human rights."

The strongly worded statement, which followed a similar explanation on Tuesday when Yeltsin turned down the bill, indicated the political sensitivity of a move that has pitted him against some of Russia's top clergymen and lawmakers.

The bill identified Orthodoxy, Islam, Buddhism and Judaism as traditional faiths in the multi-ethnic Russian Federation, awarding them full legal rights denied to other confessions including the Roman Catholic Church.
The bill would also have imposed new restrictions on foreign missionaries operating in Russia.
Patriarch Alexiy II, head of the Russian Orthodox Church, had thrown his moral weight behind the bill. He was expected to comment on Yeltsin's decision at a news conference on Thursday.
Communists, who in the Soviet era harassed and persecuted religious believers but have now become strong defenders of Russian traditions including Orthodoxy, also attacked Yeltsin.

One prominent communist deputy, Viktor Iluykhin, said Yeltsin's move showed yet again that Russia had become a protectorate of the West. U.S. senators had threatened to withhold around $200 million worth of aid if the bill passed.
Russia's parliament will reconsider the bill after its summer recess ends in September.
